newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Ministers prepare for annual battle over fish quotas.
newsitem.headline: Ministers prepare for annual battle over fish quotas.

text.p: European Union fisheries ministers are preparing for their annual battle over fish catch quotas, tyring to balance the economic needs of their fishermen with the need to safeguard scarce stocks, EU officials said on Wednesday.
They said that although the European Commission has proposed little change in quotas for most species, a scrap was still likely at the two-day meeting starting on Thursday.
"There are a number of contentious issues. It's likely to be a long night with a lot of horse trading," an Irish EU Presidency official said.
Ireland plans to hold bilateral talks with member states to discuss their demands early on Thursday before formally attacking a 17-point agenda in the afternoon.

In view of seriously depleted North Sea herring stocks, the Commission is seeking to extend emergency measures introduced in July and fix a 1997 total allowable catch (TAC) of 159,000 tonnes, roughly half the 1996 level.
It is also seeking for the first time to fix a quota for by-catches of herring by huge vessels hunting sprats for industrial processing into fish meal and oil.

A 50 percent cut in North Sea sole catches to 12,000 tonnes is also being sought to protect stocks that have dwindled to critical levels. The reduction, which would also affect fishing for plaice, would affect mainly British and Dutch fishermen.
Cod, haddock, whiting and saithe quotas off the west coast of Scotland and England are also likely to be contentious.

But officials said one of the biggest battles will be over new EU Baltic cod, herring, sprat and salmon quotas to take account of Sweden and Finland's membership of the EU and ending of their bilateral accords with Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.
Germany, Denmark and Finland strongly oppose the proposed re-allocation of fishing rights.
Another potential flashpoint is over proposed measures to halt the decline of sardine stocks off the coasts of Spain and Portugal.

Italy and Greece will be fighting hard over the introduction of quotas for bluefin tuna in the Mediterranean and Atlantic and for swordfish in the Atlantic following recommendations by international scientists.

Another innovation will be the definition of stocks eligible for flexible quota management from 1998. It enables countries to borrow up to 10 percent of next year's quota but borrowings must be paid back the following year on pain of penalties.
"It recognises the fact that the fishing season doesn't follow the calendar year," said an official, noting that cod and haddock is fished from the autumn to the spring.
Among other issues, agreement may finally be reached on a satellite fishing vessel tracking system, officials said.
But they added that there was little chance of agreeing a new multiannual fleet and fishing reduction programme.
As a result the 1992-96 scheme may be formally extended for a year or there could be a gentleman's agreement for a temporary extension while negotiations continue.
